section.title: A Resolve to Walk Blamelessly
section.sectionRationale: A royal psalm reading like David's own inaugural pledge, this hymn moves from private integrity at home to public rejection of slander and pride to daily governance in the city of the LORD, a portrait of righteous kingship that only Christ, the true and greater Son of David, fulfills without failure.
section.thesis: Because he will sing of the LORD's loving devotion and justice, the king resolves to walk with integrity in his own house, to reject every worthless and deceitful thing near him, and to purge wickedness daily from the city of the LORD.
section.frameNote: Three movements: personal vows of praise and integrity at home, verses 1-4; the rejection of slander, pride, and deceit from his presence, verses 5-7; and the daily purging of the wicked from the city of the LORD, verse 8.

units.label: I will walk with integrity of heart
units.note: personal vows of praise and integrity

verses.text: A Psalm of David. I will sing of Your loving devotion and justice; to You, O LORD, I will sing praises.
I will ponder the way that is blameless, when will You come to me? I will walk in my house with {{tamim|integrity}} of heart.
I will set no {{beliyaal|worthless thing}} before my eyes. I hate the work of those who fall away; it shall not cling to me.
A perverse heart shall depart from me; I will know nothing of evil.

units.label: No one who practices deceit
units.note: the rejection of slander, pride, and deceit

verses.text: Whoever slanders his neighbor in secret, I will put to silence; the one with haughty eyes and a proud heart, I will not endure.
My eyes favor the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me; he who walks in the way of integrity shall minister to me.
No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house; no one who tells lies shall stand in my presence.

units.label: Every morning I will remove the wicked
units.note: the daily purging of the city

verses.text: Every morning I will remove all the wicked of the land, that I may cut off every evildoer from the city of the LORD.

tamim.gloss: Blameless, complete, having integrity. The king vows to walk in his own house with this wholeness of character, a standard only fully met by Christ, the truly blameless King, Hebrews 7:26.

beliyaal.gloss: Worthless, wicked, later used as a name for the devil himself, 2 Corinthians 6:15. The king resolves to set nothing of this worthless kind before his eyes, guarding what he allows into his household and heart.

basic.context: Reading like an inaugural pledge for a new king's household and court, this psalm moves from David's own vows of personal integrity, refusing worthless things and perverse hearts, to his public rejection of slanderers and the proud, to his resolve to purge wickedness from the city of the LORD every single morning.
basic.hermeneutics: David's vows describe an ideal of righteous kingship rooted in his own historical reign, yet Scripture is honest that David himself did not perfectly keep these resolves; the psalm therefore functions both as a genuine aspiration for every leader and as a pattern that points beyond David to a King who keeps it fully.
basic.originalLanguages: The king resolves to walk in tamim, blameless integrity, within his own house, and to set no beliyaal, worthless thing, a word later applied to the devil himself, before his eyes. Personal holiness and public governance are held together as one seamless resolve.
basic.typology: David's resolve to walk blamelessly in his house, surround himself with the faithful, and purge deceit from his court anticipates Israel's ideal King as pictured in Isaiah 11:3-5, one who judges with righteousness, fully realized only in Christ, the King who is truly without sin, Hebrews 7:26.
basic.christ: Where David's own reign fell short of this psalm's ideal, most notably in his sin against Uriah and Bathsheba, Christ fulfills it perfectly as the King who 'loved righteousness and hated wickedness,' Hebrews 1:9, and whose cleansing of the temple, John 2:13-17, embodies this psalm's refusal to allow deceit or corruption in God's own house.
basic.god: God is the standard by which the king measures his own integrity, His loving devotion and justice together are the subject of the king's opening song, and it is specifically 'the city of the LORD,' not merely the king's own city, from which evil must be purged.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 17:18-20 requires Israel's king to keep God's law daily so his heart would not be lifted up in pride, the same concern this psalm expresses. Proverbs 25:5 counsels removing the wicked from the king's presence so his throne is established, echoing this psalm's resolve. Isaiah 11:3-5 pictures the ideal Messianic King who judges with righteousness. Hebrews 1:9 declares that Christ loved righteousness and hated wickedness, fulfilling this psalm's vow perfectly.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's royal resolve toward personal integrity and public righteousness, a standard David himself could not keep without failure, runs forward to Christ, the true and greater King who loved righteousness and hated wickedness without exception.

context.literary:
Psalm 101 is a string of vows. Nearly every verb is in the first person and looks forward: 'I will sing,' 'I will ponder,' 'I will walk,' 'I will set,' 'I will know nothing of evil,' 'I will put to silence,' 'I will not endure,' 'I will remove.' The grammar is not of description but of resolution, and that is what makes the psalm feel like an oath of office. It is also a psalm that moves steadily outward. It begins with the singer's mouth, verse 1, goes to his house and heart, verse 2, then to his eyes, verse 3, then to his inner life, verse 4, then to his court, verses 5 to 7, and ends at the gate of the city, verse 8. The circles widen from the self to the household to the palace to the capital.

Eyes recur as a thread. 'I will set no worthless thing before my eyes,' verse 3, the proud have 'haughty eyes,' verse 5, and 'my eyes favor the faithful,' verse 6. What the king looks at shapes whom he favours, and whom he favours shapes what his court becomes. The psalm is also concerned with where he stands and who stands near. 'That they may dwell with me,' verse 6, is matched by 'shall dwell in my house,' verse 7, and 'shall stand in my presence,' the same verse. The test of a court is who is allowed near the throne.

There is a pattern of contrasts. Verse 1 opens with two positive words, loving devotion and justice, and the rest of the psalm shows what it looks like to imitate them. The king who sings of God's chesed and mishpat will practise them. The negative vows of verses 3 to 5 and 7 and 8 are balanced by the positive ones of verses 2 and 6.

A single pair of words frames the whole, 'every morning' at the end and 'when will You come to me?' in the middle of verse 2. The psalm turns on a question to God that is unanswered, which gives the vows an aching quality: the king is promising what he cannot do unless God comes.
context.historical:
The heading names David, and the psalm reads as a king's programme at the start of his reign, which has led many to imagine it as sung at an accession or a covenant renewal. The setting can be put together from the account in Samuel. David began in Hebron and then took Jerusalem, where he established his court, and the question in verse 2, 'when will You come to me?' recalls the moment when, after the death of Uzzah, he cried, 'How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?' 2 Samuel 6:9. The bringing of the ark to Zion made the city what verse 8 calls 'the city of the LORD,' and David's household stood next to the place where God had chosen to dwell.

The psalm describes the kind of court a king of Israel was meant to keep. In the ancient Near East a king's household included officials, scribes, advisers and servants, and what he allowed near him determined the justice of his kingdom. Proverbs says the same in proverbial form: 'Remove the wicked from the king's presence, and his throne will be established in righteousness,' Proverbs 25:5, and 'If a ruler listens to lies, all his officials will be wicked,' Proverbs 29:12. The king's morning duty in verse 8 fits the picture of the king as chief judge, sitting in the gate at the start of the day to hear cases. Jeremiah's word to the house of David, 'Administer justice every morning,' Jeremiah 21:12, echoes the very word 'every morning' in this psalm.

The psalm also measures what kings should be against what they often were. The text of Samuel records David's reign as one of justice and righteousness, 2 Samuel 8:15, but also of the affair with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah, 2 Samuel 11, and of a household in which a wrong done to Tamar produced only a king who 'was furious,' 2 Samuel 13:21. The psalm thus sits above David's actual record like a standard. It was kept after David as a pattern for the kings of Judah, and a later king, hearing it, would hear both an ideal and an accusation.

The wording of verse 8 refers to 'the wicked of the land.' The city in view is Jerusalem, and the text is speaking of a civic duty, not of a campaign of conquest.
context.canonical:
Psalm 101 opens a small group of psalms of David, 101 to 103, after the long series of kingship psalms that ended with Psalm 100. After a series that celebrated God's reign, the psalm turns to the question of what kind of human king could serve under Him. The answer is one who sings of His loving devotion and justice and tries to match it.

It has strong links to the wisdom writings. The king who sifts evil with his eyes, Proverbs 20:8, the throne established by righteousness, Proverbs 16:12, and the removal of the wicked from the king's presence, Proverbs 25:5, describe the same ideal. It also has a close cousin in Psalm 15, where the person who may dwell in the LORD's tent 'walks with integrity,' has 'no slander on his tongue' and 'honors those who fear the LORD,' Psalm 15:2 to 4. Psalm 101 is Psalm 15 put in the mouth of the king, who is to be the first to meet the standard.

The promise to David in 2 Samuel 7 sets the context: a descendant who will reign forever, and whose sins will be disciplined but whose line will not be rejected, 2 Samuel 7:12 to 16. Psalm 101 is the human side of that covenant. The king who has been promised a throne is asked to keep the throne clean. The prophets then judge the kings by this standard and find them wanting, and they promise a righteous Branch who will 'reign wisely as King and will administer justice and righteousness in the land,' Jeremiah 23:5, and a king who will reign in righteousness, Isaiah 32:1.

In the New Testament the psalm's language appears in two kinds of places. The first is the cleansing of the temple, where Jesus drives out those who had made His Father's house a marketplace, John 2:14 to 17, and the disciples remember 'Zeal for Your house will consume Me.' The second is in the qualifications for church leaders in 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:7 to 9, where an overseer is to be 'above reproach,' and in Paul's instruction to 'expel the wicked man from among you,' 1 Corinthians 5:13. Hebrews 1:8 to 9 ends by saying of the Son, 'You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness,' a line that matches the psalm's vow to hate evil.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm was written for the king to sing and for the people to hear him sing. That double audience shapes what it means. To the king it is a vow before God: a promise made where the LORD can hear it, which is why the psalm begins and ends in worship and not in politics. To the people it is an announcement of the standards by which he will rule and by which they may hold him. A royal vow sung in public turns private resolution into public accountability.

The first thing the author wants grasped is that governing begins in the heart and in the home. The king is to walk with integrity 'in my house,' verse 2, before he acts in the city. Public justice that does not rest on private integrity is a fraud, and the psalm will not let the two be split. The second is that what a leader looks at and tolerates matters. The vows about eyes and about company are vows about influence, and they assume that a person becomes like those he keeps near.

The third is that justice includes both positive and negative duties. The king is not only to avoid evil but to 'favor the faithful' and bring them close, verse 6. He is to honour the good as well as remove the bad. The fourth is that the king's own desire for God's presence comes first. The question in verse 2 shows that the integrity he promises depends on God's coming to him. The author wants the hearer to see that the king's resolve is not self-confidence but a prayer wrapped in a promise.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes one king's resolutions. It does not command every believer to do what he vowed, and in particular it does not authorise private persons to 'remove all the wicked of the land' every morning. The vow in verse 8 belongs to an office: it is the work of a ruler with judicial authority over a city, exercised through courts and not through vigilante action. Christians have no such role over a civil community, and Paul says that church discipline is for those inside the church and that God will judge those outside, 1 Corinthians 5:12 to 13.

What does carry over is the pattern of personal integrity. The vows about the heart, the home, the eyes and the company are general applications that Scripture commends to everyone. Psalm 119:37 prays 'Turn my eyes away from worthless things,' and Psalm 141:3 prays for a guard over the lips. Paul gives the same standard for overseers, and more broadly believers are to be blameless and pure, Philippians 2:15. So the prescription for leaders of every kind, in a home, a company, a church or a government, is that they should start with their own lives and be careful about what they allow near them.

The psalm also has a descriptive element that the careful reader must not turn into a rule. It describes a king who swears he will keep these standards, and the history shows that kings often did not. That is a caution against reading the psalm as a guarantee that good intentions produce good rule. It is a vow, and vows can be broken.

Finally, the warning about slander and pride in verse 5 is a general moral teaching that agrees with Proverbs 6:16 to 17, where haughty eyes and a lying tongue are among the things the LORD hates. That is prescriptive for anyone in any role.

debates.question: What does 'when will You come to me?' mean in verse 2?

views.label: A longing for God's presence
views.case: After the death of Uzzah David cried out about the ark, 'How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?' 2 Samuel 6:9, and when the ark did come to Zion, the city became 'the city of the LORD.' On this reading the king pleads for God to come and dwell with him so that the integrity he promises will be possible.

views.label: A prayer for help in keeping the vow
views.case: The question stands between two vows about blamelessness and integrity, and it reads as an aside in which the king admits he cannot keep them alone. God's coming would be His help to the king, in line with the way later Scripture asks for the LORD's presence to enable obedience.

views.label: A sceptical question about whether the standard can ever be met
views.case: Some take the line as the king's sigh at the gap between what he promises and what he is, and as a hint that the ideal awaits someone else.

debates.bearing: All three readings agree that the vow depends on the LORD and not on the king alone. The psalm is best read as a promise made in need, which is how the New Testament finds it fulfilled, in One whom God came to in fullness, and in whom God came to us.

debates.question: Is the psalm a coronation vow, a regular royal liturgy, or a private resolution of David?

views.label: An accession vow
views.case: The heading says David, and the content reads like the opening of a reign, with its promise to begin every morning and its list of the things a new king will change. The early years in Jerusalem, after the ark was brought up, provide a fitting setting.

views.label: A standing liturgy for the kings of Judah
views.case: Because the psalm was preserved and sung, later kings would have used it in the temple when they took the throne or at yearly festivals, making it a pattern and not a single occasion.

views.label: A personal resolution that became Scripture
views.case: The psalm is written in the first person and could have been composed privately, as a statement of David's intentions, and then taken up by the community. Its place in the Psalter allows it to serve all these functions.

debates.bearing: The text says enough to show that it is a king's vow and no more than that, and it works under each reading. What matters for the church is that the standard it sets is high and that the New Testament treats it as met only by the Son of David.

debates.question: Is 'every morning I will remove the wicked' literal or idealised?

views.label: A literal judicial duty
views.case: The king sat as judge, and a daily hearing at the city gate, as Jeremiah 21:12 implies with 'administer justice every morning,' was part of his work. The vow is that he will not delay or neglect cases.

views.label: An ideal expressed in hyperbole
views.case: No king could remove all evildoers from a city in any period. The phrase sets up the goal, the full purification of the city of the LORD, which is also the goal of the last book, Revelation 21:27, and a daily resolve to work toward it.

debates.bearing: On either reading the verse expresses a resolve that evil should not be tolerated in the place where God's name dwells. Jesus's parable of the weeds, Matthew 13:30, teaches that the final separation belongs to Him at the harvest, which guards against using the verse to justify zeal in the wrong hands.

study.originalLanguages:
Six features of the Hebrew enrich the psalm.

First, the two words of verse 1, chesed and mishpat, which the BSB renders 'loving devotion and justice.' These are the pair that run through the Bible as the marks of God's rule. Chesed is covenant loyalty, the kind of love that keeps a commitment, and mishpat is the right ordering of a community, making things as they should be. The king sings them as attributes of the LORD, and in the rest of the psalm he tries to reflect both. What he sings in verse 1 he tries to practise in verses 2 to 8, so the opening line is the source of everything that follows.

Second, the verb in verse 2, 'I will ponder,' is from the root sakal. The form is one that means to act with insight, to behave wisely, and it often implies success that comes from attention. The BSB's 'ponder' catches the thinking, but the verb also has the sense of deliberate, careful conduct. The object is 'the way that is blameless,' derek tamim, where tamim means complete, whole, without defect. It is the word used of sacrificial animals without blemish and of people who are wholehearted with God, so the king resolves to be whole and not partial. The same word returns in verse 2's 'integrity of heart,' where the word for integrity is from the same root, tom, so the whole-hearted way is the way of a whole heart.

Third, verse 3 has 'worthless thing,' literally 'a word of worthlessness,' davar beliyaal. The noun beliyaal is a compound that seems to mean 'without worth' or 'good for nothing.' It is used of the sons of Eli, who did not know the LORD, in 1 Samuel 2:12, and Paul uses the transliterated form 'Belial' as a name for the enemy in 2 Corinthians 6:15. The BSB uses 'worthless,' and 'thing' translates the Hebrew word davar, which can mean word, matter or thing. So the king refuses to keep anything in his sight that is worthless in this deep sense, a policy or a pleasure or a scheme.

Fourth, the description of the enemy at the end of verse 3, 'those who fall away,' uses a word for turning aside or deviating. 'Perverse heart' in verse 4 is literally a twisted or crooked heart, a heart bent the wrong way. The imagery of straight and crooked contrasts with the 'way' of verses 2 and 6. The one who falls away leaves the road.

Fifth, verse 5 describes the slanderer as melashni, from the root lashan, to use the tongue. The form describes someone who slanders secretly, tongue work done out of sight. The haughty are described literally as 'high of eyes and wide of heart,' which is the Hebrew way of depicting someone who looks down on others and has room in his heart for nothing but himself. The verb for the king's response is a form from the root tsamat, which means to silence or to destroy, and the same verb appears in verse 8.

Sixth, the final verse uses the phrase labboqarim, 'every morning' or literally 'morning by morning,' a distributive form that stresses regularity. The king's zeal is to be a daily habit. The same verse uses 'cut off,' from karat, the verb used of covenants, which are 'cut,' and also of excluding someone from the community, and the object is 'the city of the LORD,' ir YHWH, a title for Jerusalem that shows its status.

typology.type: The king with a clean court, verses 2 to 7
typology.fulfillment: The psalm sets out the kind of king whose household reflects justice, but David's own court did not always meet it. Jesus is the King in whom the picture is complete: 'You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, Your God, has anointed You,' Hebrews 1:9, and He 'committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22. Where the king of the psalm vows to keep deceit away from his presence, Christ is the One in whom nothing deceitful was ever found. The type falls short because the vow was made by a man who could not keep it, whereas Christ keeps it, and brings His people into a court that is cleansed by His blood.

typology.type: The daily purging of the city of the LORD, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: The king resolves to cut off evildoers from the city of the LORD. Jesus enacts this in the temple, driving out the sellers and saying, 'My house will be called a house of prayer,' Matthew 21:12 to 13, and John records the disciples remembering 'Zeal for Your house will consume Me,' John 2:17. In the parable of the weeds He says the Son of Man will send His angels to 'weed out of His kingdom every cause of sin,' Matthew 13:41. The final purification is described in Revelation 21:27: nothing unclean will enter the city. The type falls short because the king could only remove some wicked people from one city, whereas Christ will deal with the whole.

typology.type: Those who are faithful and dwell with the king, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: The king's eyes favour the faithful so that they may dwell with him and minister to him. In Christ the promise is enlarged beyond the court to the whole people. He says where He is, there His servant will be also, John 12:26, and the book of Revelation promises that the redeemed will serve God day and night in His temple, Revelation 7:15. Believers are called a royal priesthood, 1 Peter 2:9, so the privilege of nearness to the King becomes theirs. The type falls short because the faithful of the psalm are a few officials, and the New Testament opens the same nearness to everyone who comes.

The psalm begins with the way that is blameless, and Jesus says, 'I am the way and the truth and the life,' John 14:6. The walk of integrity that the king wants to follow is found in a person who walked it without fault, and whom believers follow. The type also points to the house of God: the king walks 'in my house,' but the Son says that in the Father's house there are many rooms, John 14:2. The type falls short since the psalm treats blamelessness as a goal to work toward, while the gospel gives a righteousness from Christ to those who are not blameless, Romans 3:22.

study.christ:
Psalm 101 is the vow of a king who could not keep it, and so it asks, without saying so, for a King who could. The New Testament finds that King in Jesus, and the links are specific.

The clearest is the quotation from another royal psalm at Hebrews 1:8 to 9: 'Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness.' That line comes from Psalm 45, not from Psalm 101, but it says of the Son what Psalm 101 says the ideal king must be, one who loves what is right and hates what is wicked. The psalm's vows to hate the work of those who fall away, verse 3, and to cut off evildoers, verse 8, are the vows of a person who shares God's own attitude to sin, and Christ is the one who does.

There is also His character. The psalm's king vows to 'walk in my house with integrity of heart,' verse 2. Peter says of Jesus that He 'committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22, and the author of Hebrews says He 'was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15. The psalm's king has to hold a clean house against the pull of his own desires, and he fails, as David did. Christ holds the house, which is His Father's, without failure.

His action in the temple is the most visible fulfilment of verses 5 to 8. John records that He made a whip, drove out the sellers and overturned the tables, saying, 'How dare you turn My Father's house into a marketplace!' John 2:14 to 16, and the disciples recalled the line 'Zeal for Your house will consume Me,' John 2:17. Matthew adds the words of Isaiah and Jeremiah about a house of prayer that had become 'a den of robbers,' Matthew 21:12 to 13, which uses Jeremiah 7:11. This is the king of Psalm 101 at work in the city of the LORD, unwilling to allow deceit and greed in the place where God's name dwells. He also does what the psalm says of the faithful: He draws them to Himself. He calls His disciples to be with Him, and He says that whoever serves Him must follow Him, and where He is His servant will be, John 12:26.

The psalm also points to Christ by its question in verse 2, 'when will You come to me?' In the incarnation, God came. The Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and the answer to the king's longing turned out to be a king who was God with us. The psalm's hope that the LORD will come to a king's house is met in the coming of the Lord to His people.

The last point is judgment. The king vows to remove the wicked, and Jesus teaches that this belongs to the end: the Son of Man will send His angels to weed out every cause of sin, Matthew 13:41, and the judgment is left to the harvest, Matthew 13:30. The psalm's daily purge is fulfilled as a final one. For believers there is also a present application: they are to keep themselves pure 'as Christ is pure,' because of the hope of His appearing, 1 John 3:3.

The psalm is not a prophecy in the narrow sense. It is a model that shows what the anointed ruler ought to be, and it points to the Anointed One by the gap between the ideal and the record of every other king.
study.god:
The psalm is a human vow, but nearly everything in it is a reflection of God's own character, and it teaches about Him by the standard He asks of a king.

It shows a God whose rule is defined by loving devotion and justice together. The psalm opens with these two, and the king who wants to reflect them can do so only by holding both. A ruler who had justice without chesed would be cold, and a ruler who had chesed without mishpat would be weak. In the LORD they are one. This is a doctrine of God as a King who is neither harsh nor indulgent, whose love has backbone and whose justice has warmth, which is the picture given in Exodus 34:6 to 7.

It shows a God who cares about the private life and not only the public. The king is to be blameless 'in my house,' verse 2, and to keep his eyes clear, verse 3. The God who is addressed is one who sees what a person sets before his eyes and cares about the integrity of the heart, Psalm 139 and Proverbs 20:8 being near parallels. It would be a thin holiness that only cared for public conduct.

It shows a God who hates evil. The vows to 'hate the work of those who fall away,' verse 3, and to silence slander and pride, verse 5, are a king's effort to share God's own stance. Proverbs 6:16 lists among what the LORD hates 'haughty eyes' and 'a lying tongue,' which are exactly the two sins named here. That does not make God vindictive, since the psalm's concern is for the faithful and the poor who suffer under the proud. His hatred of evil is the other side of His love for people.

It shows a God who is present with those who love Him. The king's longing, 'when will You come to me?' reveals that the LORD is the one who comes to His servants, and the faithful of the land are those who 'dwell with me,' in the king's house, as the king dwells with God. Nearness to God is the goal of the whole psalm.

There is a tension the psalm leaves open. The God who is addressed is the one who can bring about the integrity the king promises, and the question 'when will You come to me?' suggests that He has not yet done so fully. The psalm holds together a settled confidence that the LORD is just and a real sense that the vows are not yet kept. It teaches patience, since the answer comes in His time.

For worship, the psalm teaches that praise and holiness go together. It begins with singing, 'I will sing of Your loving devotion and justice; to You, O LORD, I will sing praises,' and ends with work that matches it. Worship that is not followed by a clean home and a just hand is empty, and a clean life that does not begin in song is proud. Psalm 24:3 to 4 asks who may stand in His holy place and answers 'He who has clean hands and a pure heart,' which is the psalm's whole argument. The place where worshippers may come to the LORD is for those who have resolved, like this king, to walk with a whole heart, and the gospel tells us how such a resolve is finally kept: by the gift of a King who keeps it for us and in us.

crossReferences.note: After Uzzah died, David asked 'How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?' The fear and longing behind that cry help explain 'when will You come to me?' in Psalm 101:2, and they suggest that the psalm comes from a time when David was learning what it meant for the holy God to dwell near his house.

David reigned over all Israel and 'administered justice and righteousness for all his people.' This is a summary of the same goal as Psalm 101, and it shows that the psalm's ideal was at least partly met in his reign, before the failures recorded in the chapters that follow.

David sees Bathsheba from the roof, sends for her and sleeps with her. The set of vows in Psalm 101:3, to set no worthless thing before my eyes, is in painful contrast to what David's eyes and power did in this scene, and it shows that the vow could not be kept by resolve alone.

The person who may dwell in the LORD's tent walks with integrity, has no slander on his tongue and honours those who fear the LORD. Psalm 101 is this portrait spoken by a king, with the same concerns of speech, company and integrity, and the same verb of dwelling.

'Remove the wicked from the king's presence, and his throne will be established in righteousness.' It is the proverb form of Psalm 101:5 to 8, and it gives the reason for the king's vows: a throne is secured by the company the king keeps, and not only by his personal conduct.

'A king who sits on a throne to judge sifts out all evil with his eyes.' The eyes of the king in Psalm 101:3, 5 and 6 are the eyes of this proverb, discerning, selecting, and refusing, and the proverb shows that the image of a watchful royal eye was a recognised part of Israel's teaching on rule.

The LORD tells the house of David to 'administer justice every morning' and to rescue the victim of robbery, or His wrath will go out like fire. Here the prophet holds the dynasty to the standard of Psalm 101:8, and the word 'morning' shows that the daily practice was the standard against which they failed.

'Turn my eyes away from worthless things; revive me with Your word.' This is a prayer form of Psalm 101:3. The king vows not to set such things before his eyes, and the psalmist of Psalm 119 admits he needs God to turn his eyes, which shows the vow and the prayer belong together.

Of the Son the Father says, 'You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness.' The writer quotes a royal psalm, and the line matches what Psalm 101 wants of a king. Here the ideal is stated as the settled character of Christ, anointed above His companions.

Jesus drives out the sellers from the temple courts and the disciples remember 'Zeal for Your house will consume Me.' This is the king of Psalm 101 acting against corruption in the place of God's name, and it links the psalm's concern for the city of the LORD to Christ's own work.

An overseer must be above reproach, hospitable, a lover of good, upright, holy and disciplined. The list of qualities for church leaders draws on the pattern of Psalm 101 and of the wisdom tradition, and it shows the psalm's standard being applied to those who lead God's people in the church.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 101 lies at the point where the Bible's story asks whether a human ruler can carry out God's rule, and the answer the story gives is long and painful.

It begins with the creation of human beings to rule. In Genesis 1:26 to 28 humanity is made in God's image to have dominion, and the point of dominion is to care for the world as God would. The fall turned dominion into domination, and the first city in Scripture is built by Cain, Genesis 4:17. The history that follows is one of rulers who abuse power: Pharaoh, the kings of Canaan, and the years of the judges, when there was no king in Israel, Judges 21:25. When Israel asked for a king, the law had already said what such a king should be, Deuteronomy 17:14 to 20: one who reads the law, does not multiply power and does not think himself better than his brothers. Psalm 101 is the song of a king who is trying to be that.

David's reign is the test case. The promise in 2 Samuel 7 set a king on the throne of Israel forever, and Psalm 101 is what a godly response to that promise would sound like. But the record shows the vow failing. David's own house became a scene of adultery, murder and violence, and his sons repeated his faults. Kings after him gave the standard lip service, and the prophets called the house of David to account, Jeremiah 21:12 and 22:3. By the time of the exile the throne was empty.

The hope that remained was for a King who would do what Psalm 101 promises. Isaiah spoke of a king who would reign in righteousness, Isaiah 32:1, and Jeremiah of a righteous Branch who would reign wisely, Jeremiah 23:5. That is what the Gospels announce. The Son of David arrives, cleanses the temple, and will one day separate the weeds from the wheat, Matthew 13:41. His own life is the integrity the psalm wished for, and the life He gives His people is the means by which they too may walk in a whole-hearted way, Ephesians 2:10.

The story is not over, and the psalm still speaks to its unfinished part. Leaders in the church are to show the same qualities, 1 Timothy 3:2, and believers are to keep their own eyes and lips and company, 1 John 3:3. The last word is in Revelation, where 'nothing unclean will ever enter' the city, and only those whose names are in the Lamb's book of life, Revelation 21:27. The king's morning vow to cleanse the city is carried out in full, and the King who does it is the One who said, 'I am the way.' The singer of Psalm 101 sings with hope of a city in which every morning is the morning of a righteous reign.

quiz.q: Where does the king first resolve to walk with integrity in verse 2?

options.text: Within his own house.
options.note: The king begins with private integrity at home before ever addressing his public court or city.

options.text: In the marketplace, before merchants and traders.
options.note: The psalm's first resolve is specifically about his own house, not the marketplace.

options.text: On the battlefield, before enemy armies.
options.note: The psalm's concern in verse 2 is domestic integrity, not military conduct.

options.text: In the royal court, before foreign ambassadors.
options.note: Court matters appear later in the psalm, but the first resolve named is specifically about his own house.

quiz.q: What does the king vow to set before his eyes in verse 3?

options.text: No worthless thing.
options.note: Verse 3 records the vow, 'I will set no worthless thing before my eyes.'

options.text: Only images of past military victories.
options.note: The vow is a rejection of worthless things generally, not a specific endorsement of war imagery.

options.text: Whatever pleases the royal court.
options.note: The vow is precisely the opposite, a deliberate refusal of whatever is worthless, regardless of court preference.

options.text: Only scrolls of the law, to the exclusion of all else.
options.note: While devotion to God's law fits the psalm's spirit, the specific vow named is the rejection of worthless things, not an exclusive focus on scrolls.

quiz.q: How does the king respond to slanderers, according to verse 5?

options.text: He will put to silence whoever slanders his neighbor in secret.
options.note: Verse 5 explicitly states this resolve against secret slander.

options.text: He will reward those who bring him gossip about others.
options.note: The psalm's resolve is precisely to silence slander, not reward it.

options.text: He will ignore slander entirely as beneath his notice.
options.note: The text states an active resolve to silence slander, not passive indifference.

options.text: He will require slanderers to make a public apology only.
options.note: The psalm states he will put slanderers to silence, a stronger and more active response than simply requiring an apology.

quiz.q: What kind of people does the king favor to dwell with him and minister to him, in verse 6?

options.text: The faithful of the land, those who walk in the way of integrity.
options.note: Verse 6 explicitly favors the faithful and those walking in integrity for his household and service.

options.text: The wealthiest citizens, regardless of character.
options.note: The stated criterion is faithfulness and integrity, not wealth.

options.text: Only members of his own extended family.
options.note: The criterion given is character, faithfulness and integrity, not bloodline.

options.text: Skilled diplomats known for clever, flattering speech.
options.note: The psalm favors integrity and faithfulness specifically, in contrast to mere cleverness or flattery.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament present Christ in relation to this psalm's royal ideal?

options.text: As the King who actually loved righteousness and hated wickedness, fulfilling the psalm's vow where David himself later failed.
options.note: Hebrews 1:9 applies this very language to Christ, and His sinless life fulfills the psalm's standard without David's later failure.

options.text: As someone entirely unrelated to royal ideals of integrity or governance.
options.note: Hebrews 1:9 and other texts directly connect Christ to exactly this royal standard of righteousness.

options.text: As a King who abolishes the very concern for integrity and holiness in leadership.
options.note: Christ does not abolish this concern; He fulfills and embodies it perfectly.

options.text: As a King whose righteousness is identical in degree to David's own, no greater and no less.
options.note: Christ's righteousness surpasses David's, since Christ, unlike David, never failed to love righteousness and hate wickedness.

questions: The king's resolve begins at home, 'I will walk in my house with integrity of heart,' before it ever reaches his public life. Where is the gap widest between how you act privately and how you present yourself publicly?
The psalm vows to set 'no worthless thing' before the eyes. What specific media, habits, or influences might you need to remove from what you regularly allow yourself to see or dwell on?
The king resolves to silence slander rather than tolerate it. Where have you allowed gossip or slander a place in your conversations that this psalm would call you to actively refuse?
David himself, who wrote these vows, later failed to keep them. How does knowing this shape the way you approach your own resolutions to grow in godliness, with humility rather than self-reliance?

The psalm ends with a resolve to purge wickedness 'every morning,' a daily discipline rather than a one-time decision. What daily practice might help you renew, rather than merely make once, your own commitment to integrity?

translationNotes.note: The question 'when will You come to me?' interrupts the king's vows with a plea for God's own presence and help, showing that his resolve for integrity depends on God's enabling, not merely human willpower.
The Hebrew term rendered 'worthless thing,' beliyaal, later becomes a proper name associated with the devil himself, 2 Corinthians 6:15, 'What harmony is there between Christ and Belial.'

'Every morning' reflects the ancient Near Eastern custom of kings holding court and rendering judgments at the city gate at the start of each day, a practice attested at sites such as Dan and Lachish.
